source.paraphrase: The __proto__ property exposes the prototype chain. Reading or writing it reaches past the object's own properties into shared behavior.

invariants.why: Writing the prototype changes behavior for every object that shares it, and reading it mistakes shared behavior for own data.
invariants.fixHint: Create the object with a null prototype, or change the prototype once with the named helper at construction.
invariants.avoid: Destructuring __proto__ still reads the prototype. A quoted key with the same name is the same property.

source.work: MDN Web Docs, eval and Function
source.paraphrase: eval and the Function constructor compile a string into code at runtime. The compiled string runs with the caller's privileges.

invariants.why: A string that reaches eval becomes code with full access, so any injection in the string is an injection in the program.
invariants.fixHint: Parse the value with the parser for its format, or call the named function instead of compiling its name.
invariants.avoid: A direct eval(...) call and new Function(...) are this call. A member call whose property is eval, such as window.eval(code) or box.eval(code), is the same call, and so are parentheses or a comma expression around one of those callees, such as (0, eval)(code). A bracket call whose object is window, globalThis, self, or global and whose index is the string literal "eval" or 'eval', such as a call of window["eval"], is the same call, including parentheses, a comma expression, and optional chaining. A const, let, or var initialized to the eval identifier, including in parentheses, an assignment of that identifier to a bare local, or a parameter defaulted to it, and a later call of that name, such as const alias = eval; alias(code), is the same call. A later assignment does not remove the match. Another binding of that name inside the statement or function that follows the initializer keeps the call out of this match. A bracket call on any other object, a template index, the string eval outside a call, and a method declaration named eval are not this call.

source.paraphrase: The Promise executor runs synchronously and reports through resolve and reject. An async executor returns a second promise the constructor never observes.

invariants.why: A rejection inside an async executor settles the invisible promise, so the constructed promise never settles and the error is lost.
invariants.fixHint: Make the executor synchronous and call resolve or reject, or move the awaits into the task the executor starts.
invariants.avoid: An async function declaration as the executor has the same lost promise. Awaiting inside a synchronous executor body is fine.

source.work: Node.js documentation, event loop and concurrency
source.paraphrase: Awaiting each item inside a loop serializes work that could run together. The loop pays the full latency of every item in turn.

invariants.why: Serial awaits cost latency when tasks are independent, but can be necessary for ordering, rate limits, or backpressure.
invariants.fixHint: Confirm whether ordering, rate limits, backpressure or benchmark measurement require sequential work. Parallelize only independent tasks with an explicit concurrency budget; preserve deliberate serial behavior with a reviewed project policy.
invariants.avoid: This advisory check follows awaits only within the current function. Awaiting inside a nested callback is not an await by the enclosing loop. Unbounded Promise.all can change ordering, error and capacity behavior.

source.paraphrase: throw accepts any value, but catch branches on the value's shape. A literal carries no stack and no name the caller can match.

invariants.why: A thrown literal gives the catcher no stack and no type, so every catch falls back to comparing raw values.
invariants.fixHint: Throw an error object built for the failure, and keep the message next to the condition that raised it.
invariants.avoid: Quoting the literal differently does not make it an error. Wrapping it in parentheses does not add a stack.

source.work: MDN Web Docs, primitive wrapper objects
source.paraphrase: Calling String, Number, or Boolean as functions converts the value. Calling them with new wraps it in an object instead.

invariants.why: A wrapper object is always truthy and never equals its primitive, so equality checks and branches silently change meaning.
invariants.fixHint: Call the converter as a function with no new, and keep the result a primitive.
invariants.avoid: The Boolean wrapper is always truthy, even when it wraps false. Wrapping a different primitive has the same defect.

source.paraphrase: NaN compares unequal to every value, including NaN itself, with ==, !=, === and !==. Use Number.isNaN to test for it.

invariants.why: x === NaN is always false and x !== NaN is always true, so the guard never fires and an invalid number flows on.
invariants.fixHint: Replace the comparison with Number.isNaN(value), or !Number.isNaN(value) for the inverse.
invariants.avoid: Number.NaN is the same value. Putting NaN on the left does not change the result. The global isNaN coerces its argument first; Number.isNaN does not.

source.paraphrase: typeof returns one of undefined, object, boolean, number, bigint, string, symbol or function.

invariants.why: Comparing typeof with any other string is always false, so the branch is dead and the value the check was meant to stop gets through.
invariants.fixHint: Compare with one of the eight typeof results. Use value === null for null and Array.isArray(value) for arrays.
invariants.avoid: typeof never returns null, array, date or integer. Swapping the operands or writing the string as a template literal is the same comparison. Comparing with a variable is not checked.

source.paraphrase: forEach expects a synchronous function and does not wait for promises an async callback returns.

invariants.why: The caller continues before any callback finishes, and a rejected callback becomes an unhandled rejection instead of an error the caller sees.
invariants.fixHint: Use await Promise.all(items.map(async (item) => ...)) for independent work, or for...of with await when order matters.
invariants.avoid: A function expression instead of an arrow, or optional chaining on the receiver, is the same call. A sync callback that starts a promise is outside this rule. Only a forEach call used as a bare statement is reported; an awaited stream forEach is allowed. for...of with await is serial, which JS-AWAIT-001 advises on.

source.paraphrase: A return in the finally block becomes the result of the whole try statement, regardless of returns in try or catch, including when catch throws.

invariants.why: A return in finally discards the try block's result and swallows any thrown error, so a failure looks like success.
invariants.fixHint: Keep finally for cleanup. Return from try or catch, or after the whole try statement.
invariants.avoid: A return inside a nested try or catch within finally still completes the finally. A return inside a callback defined in finally is a different function and is not reported.

source.paraphrase: Comparing a variable against itself is usually an error, either a typo or an incorrect check for NaN.

invariants.why: Comparing an identifier or member expression to itself is tautological (or always false for inequality), and indicates a typo or broken logic. Use Number.isNaN() for NaN checks.
invariants.fixHint: Compare against the intended target variable, or use Number.isNaN(x) if testing for NaN.
invariants.avoid: Do not compare x === x or x !== x to test for NaN; use Number.isNaN().

source.paraphrase: Negating the left operand of in or instanceof is almost always a mistake because operator precedence binds ! first.

invariants.why: In JavaScript, !key in obj parses as (!key) in obj, evaluating key to a boolean and checking if 'true' or 'false' exists on obj.
invariants.fixHint: Wrap the expression in parentheses: !(key in obj) or !(obj instanceof Cls).
invariants.avoid: Do not rely on implicit precedence when negating binary relational operators.
